vignette: Riley's eyes still flinch when he walks past the kitchen where his ex-wife used to burn dinner on purpose, just to spite him. The smell of charred food instantly transports him back to those nights, when her anger seemed to simmer like a pot about to boil over. He tries not to think about it, but the memories linger, infused in the scent that wafts from his neighbor's kitchen or the diner down the street. Even on jobs as a plumber, when he encounters burnt wiring or overheated pipes, Riley feels a jolt of anxiety. It started three years ago, when his then-wife began to turn violent during their arguments. One night, she had pushed him against the stove, and he remembered the searing pain as his arm grazed the hot surface. After that, every disagreement ended with him walking on eggshells, never knowing when her anger would escalate into physical aggression. He learned to recognize the signs - the tightening of her jaw, the flashing in her eyes - but it didn't help. She'd lash out anyway. Riley's strategy was avoidance. He dodged confrontations, sidestepped discussions about their problems, and worked late hours to minimize time at home. But even when he wasn't there, the arguments followed him. His wife would call or text, her voice raised in anger, leaving him shaken for hours afterward. He began to dread hearing from her, especially when she'd calm down and talk sweetly, as if nothing was wrong. To cope with his insomnia, Riley developed a habit of staying up until the early morning hours, watching TV or browsing his phone to distract himself from thoughts of the past. It wasn't just the memories that plagued him - it was the what-ifs. What if he'd fought back? What if he'd left sooner? The questions swirled in his head like a toxic soup. When they finally divorced, Riley thought he could put the experience behind him. He threw himself into work and started spending more time with friends, trying to shake off the lingering fear of confrontation. However, avoiding certain places - especially their old apartment complex - had become second nature. Driving past the building made his heart rate spike; walking by would be unbearable. Lately, though, even small expressions of anger from others have begun to unsettle Riley. A coworker's exasperated sigh or a stranger's loud voice in line at the grocery store makes him tense up, bracing for impact. It's as if he's perpetually waiting for someone to blow their top. It was this hyper-vigilance that finally led Riley to seek help. One evening, his wife - now ex-wife - appeared at his doorstep, wanting to discuss some trivial matter related to the divorce settlement. Her calm demeanor didn't fool him; beneath it, he sensed the familiar undercurrent of anger. This time, though, something was different. As she stood in his doorway, speaking softly but with an edge, Riley felt a spark of recognition: this wasn't just about her anymore - it was about how he'd let the past dictate his life. His wife left after their conversation, leaving Riley shaken and exhausted. The realization dawned on him that night - as he lay awake once again, replaying the encounter in his head - that he couldn't outrun or out-avoid this any longer. He needed help to face what had happened and break free from the grip of those memories. Riley's marriage counselor wife now has her own personal counselor
